transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-11
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Artifacts referenced: shared spreadsheet (https://redwood.app/benchmarks/novushealth-plan.xlsx), repo snippet (https://github.com/redwood/harness-adapters/tree/example), security pack (link sent in chat)

Summary:
Quick scoping call to align on benchmark success criteria, clarify streaming vs non-streaming behavior for their conversational assistant, and agree on harness integration tasks and timelines for a 3-week pilot. Customer wants throughput and 95/99 latency numbers for both hosted and Dedicated configurations plus an integration plan for the customer scripts.

Topics:
- workload shape and percentiles (p95/p99, prompt length distrib)
- streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs (tail latency, cost)
- harness adapter and script expectations (auth, batching, error handling)
- success criteria and acceptance tests
- pilot timeline and security gating (VPC, SOC2 docs)

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. With me are Liam and Jin, their se and platform se. Can you see the agenda in the chat?
[00:23] Priya Rao: Yep thanks Maya, Priya here. Quick intro: NovusHealth is trying to move our triage assistant off the current prototype and we want to evaluate production economics and latency under real traffic shapes.
[00:35] Daniel Kim: Daniel, SRE - we'll own the harness and run the load clusters, liaise with infra.
[00:41] Sara Lopez: Sara, product - I'm mostly around success criteria and timelines.
[00:48] Maya Patel: Great. High level goal: get a clear benchmark plan that shows cost/throughput/latency and prove a streaming fallback approach where if streaming tail spikes we fall back to a non-streaming route to meet SLAs.
[01:05] Liam O'Rourke: Quick intro from me, I'll help with the harness adapter and metrics collection. We usually recommend running both streaming and non-streaming waveforms in the same harness runs so you can compare end-to-end latency and token cost given your prompt mix.
[01:22] Omar El-Sayed: Omar here - data eng, I'll help sanitize traces and produce the sample requests. Couple quick q's up front: what's the recommended request concurrency shape? We have spikes at start of business day and a mid-day plateau.
[01:36] Jin Park: For spikes we advise a mix of ramping fanout tests and steady-state sustained throughput. We'll want short bursts at peak concurrency to reproduce cold-KV-cache effects and then a ~30 minute plateau to gather p95 and p99.
[01:50] Priya Rao: On prompt distribution, we have roughly 70% short prompts (<40 tokens output), 20% medium (40-200) and 10% long (200-800). Does Redwood need those exact numbers to size batchers?
[02:05] Liam O'Rourke: Yes. We use that distribution to tune batching windows and kernel selection. For streaming vs non-streaming: streaming reduces perceived latency for long outputs but increases throughput variability and can hurt amortized GPU utilization if token rates are uneven.
[02:28] Daniel Kim: For our SLAs we want p95 end-to-end latency for short prompts under 250ms and p99 under 500ms. For long prompts we'll accept higher but want to quantify. Is that feasible on hosted?
[02:43] Jin Park: On hosted it's possible for short prompts depending on model family and quantization. We'll run a baseline with the open Llama variant and a slightly larger optimized model for comparison. Dedicated will give more predictable tail latencies since you control the pool.
[02:59] Priya Rao: Cost is also a big factor - can you show token-level cost and how batching affects it?
[03:07] Liam O'Rourke: Absolutely — our harness will emit token cost estimates per request and aggregate cost per 1M tokens. Expect to see cost reductions with larger batch sizes; we'll propose a few quantization profiles to test.
[03:19] Sara Lopez: Walk me through the streaming fallback flow. We don't want partial responses to confuse downstream systems.
[03:27] Maya Patel: Good question. The pattern we propose: default to streaming for long responses. If the runtime detects streaming tail latency degradation for X seconds (configurable threshold), route new requests to a non-streaming variant pinned to a Dedicated pool or lower concurrency node. That gives stable p95/p99 for new requests while existing streams finish.
[03:52] Priya Rao: So it's a routing policy? Does it require the client to do anything?
[03:57] Liam O'Rourke: Minimal client changes: the client must support both streaming and non-streaming endpoints and a small handshake header we use to tag streaming sessions. We can provide an adapter patch for your current client.
[04:10] Omar El-Sayed: About the harness adapter — what auth flows do you support? We run in a VPC and need mTLS + token rotation.
[04:18] Jin Park: We support API keys, signed mTLS, and can integrate with your internal vault for token rotation. For Private deployments we can use customer-managed KMS and HSM as well.
[04:30] Daniel Kim: We'll need SOC2 artifacts before we hand over traces — typical ask.
[04:35] Maya Patel: Understood. We'll share the security pack (SOC2 report, data handling, audit log sample) after this call. It's in the chat.
[04:42] Priya Rao: For the harness itself, can you show an example of handling retries and 429s? We want deterministic behavior in the benchmarks.
[04:50] Liam O'Rourke: Our recommended pattern: client retries only for idempotent operations and uses exponential backoff for 429s with jitter. For benchmarks we simulate 429s to measure backoff recovery but keep them off in acceptance runs. We'll include the harness config that toggles these behaviors.
[05:10] Sara Lopez: Success criteria proposal: 1) p95 latency short prompts < 250ms hosted or Dedicated; 2) p99 short prompts < 600ms for hosted, <400ms for Dedicated; 3) token cost delta between hosted and dedicated within X% (we should define X); 4) integration adapter in repo and runbook. Thoughts?
[05:35] Jin Park: Sounds good. For X let's start with 20% delta allowed; we can tighten based on pilot.
[05:42] Priya Rao: We'll sign up for 3-week pilot. Weeks: week1 dataset ingestion + harness setup, week2 run synthetic + customer script runs, week3 tune and acceptance. Can you meet that?
[05:56] Maya Patel: Yes. We propose a kickoff this Thursday for the hands-on harness session and we'll drive week1 tasks.
[06:03] Daniel Kim: On dataset ingestion — we'll provide anonymized request traces. Any preferred format?
[06:09] Liam O'Rourke: JSONL with fields: prompt, role (system/user), expected tokens estimate, timestamp. We'll provide a template in the spreadsheet.
[06:19] Priya Rao: Regarding benchmarks — we want both streaming and non-streaming runs for each model. Should they be in the same run or separate?
[06:26] Jin Park: Separate runs are cleaner for analysis. We'll run: baseline (no batching), steady-state batching, streaming enabled, streaming with fallback routing enabled. Each run will include a ramp, plateau, and cool-down, about 40 min total per model per waveform.
[06:46] Omar El-Sayed: That multiplies total run time. If we test three models and four waveforms that's 12 runs times 40 min = 8 hours. Can we parallelize?
[06:56] Liam O'Rourke: We can parallelize across Dedicated pools or stagger runs across days. For Hosted it's rate-limited per seat; we'll coordinate a reserved window. Suggest we prioritize two model variants first, then expand.
[07:14] Sara Lopez: For acceptance we'll need dashboards. Can you provide per-route p50/p95/p99, token cost, and error rates?
[07:23] Jin Park: Yes, we'll spin up a Grafana dashboard with per-route panels and raw trace links. We'll also push aggregated CSVs to the shared drive after each run.
[07:32] Priya Rao: A few gotchas: our downstream ingestion expects a JSON object per completion (structured output). We saw partial streaming chunks break the consumer. How is that handled?
[07:44] Liam O'Rourke: We recommend stream framing: each chunk is a complete JSON patch or we only stream text and emit final structured JSON via a finalize endpoint. We'll prototype both in the adapter so you can test.
[07:58] Daniel Kim: Do you support real-time KV cache warm-up between runs? We want to measure cold vs warmed KV cache effects since our assistant has a heavy prefix cache.
[08:06] Jin Park: Yes — harness supports explicit KV cache priming and a warm-up phase. We'll include runs with cold cache and with a warm cache to capture tail latency differences.
[08:18] Priya Rao: About metrics: we'd like 95th percentile for tail-latency measured at the client side (end-to-end) not just service-side. Is that standard?
[08:27] Maya Patel: Absolutely. The harness captures client-side metrics; we'll correlate with service-side telemetry. Client-side p95 is what you'll use for SLAs.
[08:35] Sara Lopez: On data residency — we may require EU region hosting for a subset. Is that something you can test?
[08:41] Jin Park: We can run jobs in EU regions for hosted and switch dedicated pools regionally. We'll document any perf delta due to region placement.
[08:51] Omar El-Sayed: Any known model families that are bad for streaming? We use some heavy longform models for summarization and want to avoid ones with pathological token emission behaviors.
[09:00] Liam O'Rourke: Some decoder-only large models emit tokens in bursts which affects streaming smoothness. We'll test model variants and report chunked emission patterns as part of the streaming profile.
[09:15] Priya Rao: OK next steps recap from our side: we'll sanitize traces and send the top 25 prompts plus a 24h sample.
[09:23] Daniel Kim: I'll check the VPC peering window and firewall rules and confirm next Tuesday.
[09:28] Maya Patel: From Redwood we'll share: benchmark plan spreadsheet, harness adapter example, security pack, and a proposed pilot schedule. We'll also open a short lived sandbox token and a repo link for the adapter.
[09:46] Sara Lopez: One last question — how do you handle billing for pilot runs? We don't want surprises.
[09:51] Maya Patel: We'll provide a capped pilot credit for the first 3 weeks and detailed token accounting in the dashboard. Any consumption beyond the cap will require pre-approval.
[09:59] Priya Rao: Good. If we get acceptable p95/p99 numbers and cost profile, we'll move to a 6-month dedicated commitment.
[10:07] Maya Patel: Great. We'll aim to have the harness session Thursday 10am your time. I'll send calendar invites after the call.
[10:15] (end of call)

Notes on transcripts and artifacts: the shared spreadsheet contains the run matrix and placeholders for expected p50/p95/p99; the repo has an example Node and Python adapter. Security docs were dropped in chat as a link.

- Liam: push harness adapter example, streaming fallback demo (by 2026-04-14)
